# option_operations - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/option-operations/

## Expand description

`option-operations` provides traits and auto-implementations to
improve arithmetic operations usability when dealing with `Option`s.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Dealing with two `Option`s, can lead to verbose expressions:

```
let lhs = Some(1u64);
let rhs = Some(u64::MAX);
assert_eq!(
    lhs.zip(rhs).map(|(lhs, rhs)| lhs.saturating_add(rhs)),
    Some(u64::MAX),
);
```
Thanks to the trait [ OptionSaturatingAdd](https://docs.rs/add/trait.OptionSaturatingAdd.html) we can write:

```
assert_eq!(
    lhs.opt_saturating_add(rhs),
    Some(u64::MAX),
);
```
The trait can also be used with the inner type:

```
assert_eq!(
    lhs.opt_saturating_add(u64::MAX),
    Some(u64::MAX),
);
assert_eq!(
    1.opt_saturating_add(rhs),
    Some(u64::MAX),
);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#alternative-to-partialord-for-optiont)Alternative to `PartialOrd` for `Option<T>`

Another purpose is to workaround the `PartiaOrd` implementation
for `Option<T>`, which uses the declaration order of the variants
for `Option`. `None` appearing before `Some(_)`, it results in
the following behavior:

```
let some_0 = Some(0);
let none: Option<u64> = None;
assert_eq!(none.partial_cmp(&some_0), Some(Ordering::Less));
assert_eq!(some_0.partial_cmp(&none), Some(Ordering::Greater));
```
In some cases, we might consider that `None` reflects a value which
is not defined and thus can not be compared with `Some(_)`.

```
assert_eq!(none.opt_cmp(&some_0), None);
assert_eq!(some_0.opt_cmp(&none), None);
```
Of course, this is consistent with other usual comparisons:

```
assert_eq!(none.opt_lt(&some_0), None);
assert_eq!(none.opt_min(some_0), None);
```

# option-operations 0.6.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/option-operations/latest

# option-operations

`option-operations` provides traits and auto-implementations to
improve arithmetic operations usability when dealing with `Option`s.

## Example

Dealing with two `Option`s, can lead to verbose expressions:

```
let lhs = Some;
let rhs = Some;
assert_eq!;
```
Thanks to the trait `OptionSaturatingAdd` we can write:

```
assert_eq!;
```
The trait can also be used with the inner type:

```
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
```
## Alternative to `PartialOrd` for `Option<T>`

Another purpose is to workaround the `PartiaOrd` implementation
for `Option<T>`, which uses the declaration order of the variants
for `Option`. `None` appearing before `Some(_)`, it results in
the following behavior:

```
let some_0 = Some;
let none:  = None;
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
```
In some cases, we might consider that `None` reflects a value which
is not defined and thus can not be compared with `Some(_)`.

```
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
```
Of course, this is consistent with other usual comparisons:

```
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
```

# pastey - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/pastey/^0.2.0/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#macros-for-all-your-token-pasting-needs)Macros for all your token pasting needs

`pastey` is the fork of `paste` and is aimed to be a drop-in replacement with additional features for
`paste` crate

## Migrating from `paste` crate

Migrating from `paste` crate to `pastey` is super simple, just change the following
in your `Cargo.toml`

```
[dependencies]
- paste = "1"
+ pastey = "*" # Or any specific version of pastey
```
Or even better way:

```
[dependencies]
- paste = "1"
+ paste = { package = "pastey", version = "*" }
```
[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

Add `pastey` as your dependency in `Cargo.toml`

```
[dependencies]
# TODO: Replace with latest version available on crates.io
pastey = "*"
```
This approach works with any Rust compiler 1.54+.

[§](https://docs.rs#pasting-identifiers)Pasting identifiers

Within the `paste!` macro, identifiers inside `[<`…`>]` are pasted together to
form a single identifier.

```
use pastey::paste;
paste! {
    // Defines a const called `QRST`.
    const [<Q R S T>]: &str = "success!";
}
fn main() {
    assert_eq!(
        paste! { [<Q R S T>].len() },
        8,
    );
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#more-elaborate-example)More elaborate example

The next example shows a macro that generates accessor methods for some struct fields. It demonstrates how you might find it useful to bundle a paste invocation inside of a macro_rules macro.

```
use pastey::paste;
macro_rules! make_a_struct_and_getters {
    ($name:ident { $($field:ident),* }) => {
        // Define a struct. This expands to:
        //
        //     pub struct S {
        //         a: String,
        //         b: String,
        //         c: String,
        //     }
        pub struct $name {
            $(
                $field: String,
            )*
        }
        // Build an impl block with getters. This expands to:
        //
        //     impl S {
        //         pub fn get_a(&self) -> &str { &self.a }
        //         pub fn get_b(&self) -> &str { &self.b }
        //         pub fn get_c(&self) -> &str { &self.c }
        //     }
        paste! {
            impl $name {
                $(
                    pub fn [<get_ $field>](&self) -> &str {
                        &self.$field
                    }
                )*
            }
        }
    }
}
make_a_struct_and_getters!(S { a, b, c });
fn call_some_getters(s: &S) -> bool {
    s.get_a() == s.get_b() && s.get_c().is_empty()
}
let s = S {
    a: String::from("x"),
    b: String::from("x"),
    c: String::new(),
 };
 assert!(call_some_getters(&s));
 let s2 = S {
     a: String::from("x"),
     b: String::from("y"),
     c: String::new(),
 };
 assert!(!call_some_getters(&s2));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#case-conversion)Case conversion

The `pastey` crate supports the following case modfiers:

| Modifier | Description |
|---|---|
| `$var:lower` | Lower Case |
| `$var:upper` | Upper Case |
| `$var:snake` | Snake Case |
| `$var:camel`or`$var:upper_camel` | Upper Camel Case |
| `$var:lower_camel` | Lower Camel Case [#4](https://github.com/AS1100K/pastey/issues/4) |
| `$var:camel_edge` | Covers Edge cases of Camel Case. [#3](https://github.com/AS1100K/pastey/issues/3) |

**NOTE: The pastey crate is going to be a drop in replacement to paste crate,
and will not change the behaviour of existing modifier like  lower, upper,
snake and camel. For modifying the behaviour new modifiers will be created,
like camel_edge**

You can also use multiple of these modifers like `$var:snake:upper` would give you
`SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE`.

Example

```
use pastey::paste;
paste! {
    const [<LIB env!("CARGO_PKG_NAME"):snake:upper>]: &str = "libpastey";
    let _ = LIBPASTEY;
}
```
The precise Unicode conversions are as defined by [ str::to_lowercase](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html#method.to_lowercase) and

[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html#method.to_uppercase)

`str::to_uppercase`[§](https://docs.rs#replace-modifier)Replace modifier

The `replace` modifier allows you to perform string replacement on identifiers,
using the same semantics as [ str::replace](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html#method.replace). This is useful for transforming
identifiers by removing or substituting substrings.

```
use pastey::paste;
macro_rules! m {
    ($(($command:ident, $from:ident)),+) => {
        paste! {
            $(pub struct $command {})*
            pub enum Command {
                $(
                    [< $command:replace($from, "") >] ( $command )
                ),*
            }
        }
    }
}
m! {
    (CommandFoo, Command),
    (CommandBar, Command),
    (HelloWorld, Hello)
}
let command_bar = Command::Bar(CommandBar {});
let command_foo = Command::Foo(CommandFoo {});
let command_hello = Command::World(HelloWorld {});
```
[§](https://docs.rs#raw-identifier-generation)Raw Identifier Generation

`pastey` now supports raw identifiers using a special raw mode. By prefixing a
token with `#` inside the paste syntax, it treats that token as a raw identifier.

```
use pastey::paste;
macro_rules! define_struct_and_impl {
    ($name:ident $(- $name_tail:ident)*) => {
        paste!{
            struct [< # $name:camel $( $name_tail)* >]; // '#' signals a raw identifier
            impl [< # $name:camel $( $name_tail)* >] {
                fn [< # $name:snake $( _ $name_tail:snake)* >]() {}
            }
        }
    }
}
define_struct_and_impl!(loop);
define_struct_and_impl!(loop - xyz);
fn test_fn() {
    let _ = Loop::r#loop();
    let _ = Loopxyz::loop_xyz();
}
test_fn();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#pasting-documentation-strings)Pasting documentation strings

Within the `paste!` macro, arguments to a #[doc …] attribute are implicitly
concatenated together to form a coherent documentation string.

```
use pastey::paste;
macro_rules! method_new {
    ($ret:ident) => {
        paste! {
            #[doc = "Create a new `" $ret "` object."]
            pub fn new() -> $ret { $ret {} }
        }
    };
}
pub struct Pastey {}
method_new!(Pastey);  // expands to #[doc = "Create a new `Paste` object"]
let _ = new();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#credits)Credits

This crate is the fork of

[and I appreciate the efforts of](https://github.com/dtolnay/paste)`paste`[@dtolnay](https://github.com/dtolnay)and other contributors.[§](https://docs.rs#license)License

Licensed under either of

[Apache License, Version 2.0](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-APACHE)or[MIT license](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-MIT)at your option.Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally submitted for inclusion in this crate by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.

# option_operations - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/option-operations/latest/target-redirect/option_operations/

## Expand description

`option-operations` provides traits and auto-implementations to
improve arithmetic operations usability when dealing with `Option`s.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Dealing with two `Option`s, can lead to verbose expressions:

```
let lhs = Some(1u64);
let rhs = Some(u64::MAX);
assert_eq!(
    lhs.zip(rhs).map(|(lhs, rhs)| lhs.saturating_add(rhs)),
    Some(u64::MAX),
);
```
Thanks to the trait [ OptionSaturatingAdd](https://docs.rs/add/trait.OptionSaturatingAdd.html) we can write:

```
assert_eq!(
    lhs.opt_saturating_add(rhs),
    Some(u64::MAX),
);
```
The trait can also be used with the inner type:

```
assert_eq!(
    lhs.opt_saturating_add(u64::MAX),
    Some(u64::MAX),
);
assert_eq!(
    1.opt_saturating_add(rhs),
    Some(u64::MAX),
);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#alternative-to-partialord-for-optiont)Alternative to `PartialOrd` for `Option<T>`

Another purpose is to workaround the `PartiaOrd` implementation
for `Option<T>`, which uses the declaration order of the variants
for `Option`. `None` appearing before `Some(_)`, it results in
the following behavior:

```
let some_0 = Some(0);
let none: Option<u64> = None;
assert_eq!(none.partial_cmp(&some_0), Some(Ordering::Less));
assert_eq!(some_0.partial_cmp(&none), Some(Ordering::Greater));
```
In some cases, we might consider that `None` reflects a value which
is not defined and thus can not be compared with `Some(_)`.

```
assert_eq!(none.opt_cmp(&some_0), None);
assert_eq!(some_0.opt_cmp(&none), None);
```
Of course, this is consistent with other usual comparisons:

```
assert_eq!(none.opt_lt(&some_0), None);
assert_eq!(none.opt_min(some_0), None);
```

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

---

# Badges

Source: https://docs.rs/about/badges

Docs.rs no longer has its own badges. Consider using [shields.io](https://shields.io) instead.

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (c397dae80 2026-07-02)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

---

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# xpile_llm - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/xpile-llm/0.1.615/xpile_llm/

## Expand description

LLM invocation + content-addressed cache.

Cache key is `sha256(source_bytes || xpile_version || model_id || skills_hash)`.
On cache hit, returns the exact bytes stored — byte-identical across
runs and machines. This is what makes the stochastic agent loop
reproducible at the artifact level.

See `contracts/xpile-determinism-v1.yaml` (TODO).

# dynstaller

## Installing Windows Sandbox

Instructions are provided by Microsoft [here](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/application-security/application-isolation/windows-sandbox/windows-sandbox-install). Otherwise, open a PowerShell terminal as an administrator and run the following command:

```
Enable-WindowsOptionalFeature -FeatureName "Containers-DisposableClientVM" -All -Online
```
## Running Windows Sandbox

To run a .wsb (Windows Sandbox configuration file), you can double-click the file in File Explorer or pass it via command line:

```
"C:\Windows\System32\WindowsSandbox.exe" "C:\path\to\your\file.wsb"
```

Full user guides for dynstaller are available [online](https://dynstaller.readthedocs.io)
and in the [docs](https://docs.rs/docs) directory.

For questions or support, please create a new discussion on [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/LLNL/dynstaller/discussions/categories/q-a),
or [open an issue](https://github.com/LLNL/dynstaller/issues/new/choose) for bug reports and feature requests.

Contributions are welcome. Bug fixes or minor changes are preferred via a
pull request to the [dynstaller GitHub repository](https://github.com/LLNL/dynstaller).
For more information on contributing see the [CONTRIBUTING](https://docs.rs/CONTRIBUTING.md) file.

# openlineage_client - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/openlineage-client/0.0.4/openlineage_client/

## Expand description

Transport-agnostic [OpenLineage](https://openlineage.io) event model and emit client.

This crate owns the emission side of OpenLineage: the [ RunEvent](https://docs.rs/event/struct.RunEvent.html) model and
its typed facets, a pluggable

[sink, and a non-blocking](https://docs.rs/transport/trait.Transport.html)

`Transport`[that hands events to a background drain task. It has](https://docs.rs/client/struct.OpenLineageClient.html)

`OpenLineageClient`**no DataFusion (or any engine) dependency**— engine integrations such as

[build on top of it, and so can any other emitter.](https://docs.rs/datafusion-openlineage)

`datafusion-openlineage`[§](https://docs.rs#the-transport-seam)The transport seam

How events are published is deliberately unspecified. The [ Transport](https://docs.rs/transport/trait.Transport.html) trait
is the only seam: an implementation might POST to a spec-compliant OpenLineage
REST endpoint, publish to a Kafka topic, or do anything else. The crate ships

[,](https://docs.rs/transport/struct.NoopTransport.html)

`NoopTransport`[, and — behind the](https://docs.rs/transport/struct.ConsoleTransport.html)

`ConsoleTransport``http` feature —
[, which posts to an (optionally authenticated) HTTP endpoint via](https://docs.rs/cloud/struct.CloudClientTransport.html)

`CloudClientTransport``olai-http`. To target something else, implement [.](https://docs.rs/transport/trait.Transport.html)

`Transport`[§](https://docs.rs#non-blocking-emission)Non-blocking emission

[ OpenLineageClient::emit](https://docs.rs/client/struct.OpenLineageClient.html#method.emit) never blocks and never applies back-pressure: it
hands the event to a bounded channel drained by a background task. If the
queue is full the event is dropped with a warning — lineage must never slow or
break the host workload. Call

[before exit to drain queued events and flush the transport.](https://docs.rs/client/struct.OpenLineageClient.html#method.shutdown)

`OpenLineageClient::shutdown`[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use std::sync::Arc;
use openlineage_client::{ConsoleTransport, OpenLineageClient};
let client = OpenLineageClient::new(Arc::new(ConsoleTransport));
client.emit(event);          // non-blocking
client.shutdown().await;     // drain + flush before exit
```
[§](https://docs.rs#environment)Environment

[ OpenLineageClient::from_env](https://docs.rs/client/struct.OpenLineageClient.html#method.from_env) and

[read the standard OpenLineage environment variables, so an integration can wire itself up from the environment the rest of the ecosystem already uses:](https://docs.rs/config/struct.OpenLineageConfig.html#method.from_env)

`OpenLineageConfig::from_env`| Variable | Read by | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `OPENLINEAGE_URL` | `OpenLineageClient::from_env` | Base URL of the endpoint (unset → no-op client) |
| `OPENLINEAGE_ENDPOINT` | `OpenLineageClient::from_env` | Path appended to the URL (default `/api/v1/lineage`) |
| `OPENLINEAGE_API_KEY` | `OpenLineageClient::from_env` | Bearer token, if set |
| `OPENLINEAGE_NAMESPACE` | `OpenLineageConfig::from_env` | Default job namespace |
| `OPENLINEAGE_TIMEOUT_MS` | `OpenLineageConfig::from_env` | Per-request transport timeout |
| `OPENLINEAGE_PARENT_ID`/`OPENLINEAGE_PARENT_*` | `LineageContext::from_env` | Parent run facet |

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use client::`- [ClientError](https://docs.rs/client/enum.ClientError.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [client](https://docs.rs/client/index.html)
- The OpenLineage client: a non-blocking emit front-end over a `Transport`
- [cloud](https://docs.rs/cloud/index.html)
- Default HTTP transport backed by `olai_http::CloudClient`
- [config](https://docs.rs/config/index.html)
- Static configuration shared across emitted events.

- Top-level orchestration context contributed per emitted run.

- OpenLineage facet types.

- OpenLineage dataset naming-spec mapping.
- [transport](https://docs.rs/transport/index.html)
- Pluggable sink for OpenLineage events.

# headwaters_client - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/headwaters-client/0.0.4/headwaters_client/

## Expand description

An async Rust client for the [Headwaters](https://github.com/open-lakehouse/headwaters)
read API.

[ HeadwatersClient](https://docs.rs/struct.HeadwatersClient.html) wraps the generated ConnectRPC client with one method
per read RPC, returning owned response messages. Build one from a base URL:

```
use headwaters_client::HeadwatersClient;
let client = HeadwatersClient::connect("http://localhost:8091")?;
// Browse, then walk the lineage graph.
let dataset = client.get_dataset("analytics", "orders").await?;
let node = headwaters_client::dataset_node_id("analytics", "orders");
let graph = client.get_lineage(&node, 2).await?;
println!("{} reachable nodes", graph.graph.len());
```
The open-ended `facets` / `data` / `fields` / `events` fields on the response
messages are `google.protobuf.Struct`; [ struct_to_json](https://docs.rs/types/fn.struct_to_json.html) turns one into a

[.](https://docs.rs/serde_json/1.0.150/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_json/value/enum.Value.html)

`serde_json::Value`## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

# fugazi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/fugazi/0.7.0/fugazi/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#fugazi)Fugazi

A library of technical-analysis (TA) building blocks designed around
*incremental* computation. Every primitive owns its internal state and is
advanced one sample at a time through `update()`, carrying just enough
intermediate state to produce the next output in O(1) (or close to it).
This makes the same code usable for live streaming and batch backtesting.

The crate has three composable layers:

- `Indicator`- *sources*. Each incrementally produces a- `Real`- **owns its own input source**, so composition is just nesting constructors:- `Ema::new(Current::close(), 20)`is the EMA-20 of the close,- `Ema::new(Sma::new(src, 10), 20)`an EMA of an SMA. Outputs are exposed as public fields refreshed every- `Indicator::update`- `value`. Leaf sources (- `Value`- `Identity`- `Current::*`for candle fields) terminate the chain. Bar indicators (- `Atr`- `Adx`- `Candle`
- `Signal`- *composable*booleans, which are simply- `Indicator`- `Output`is- `bool`. Comparison signals are built from two sources, so a condition like “RSI over 70” is a single object; combine them further with the- `BoolIndicatorExt`- `and`/- `or`/- `xor`/- `not`/- `changed`).- `Signal`itself names a- `bool`indicator fed a- `Candle`- `Box<dyn Signal>`.
- `Strategy`- *decision*layer. Unlike the pure layers below it, a strategy- *acts*, in two steps:- `update`- `trade`- `Wallet`- `wallet.set`/- `close`, with a- `Side`- `Size`- `Wallet::update`- `Reference`- `Units`- `Wallet`- *trait*, so the same strategy runs against a- `PaperWallet`

```
use fugazi::prelude::*;
use fugazi::indicators::{Identity, Rsi};
// "RSI(14) over 70" as a single bool-valued indicator over a raw price
// stream. Indicators own their source, so `Identity` feeds it into the RSI.
let mut overbought = Rsi::new(Identity::new(), 14).above(70.0);
for price in [44.0, 44.3, 44.1, 43.6, 44.3, 44.8, 45.1, 45.6] {
    overbought.update(price);
}
let _ = overbought.is_true();
```

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [assets](https://docs.rs/assets/index.html)
- Asset resolution. Backends fetch templates, reference docs, images, etc.
through this trait — never `std::fs`. The default impl bakes the built-in catalog in via`rust-embed`; consumers wrap or replace it.
- [backends](https://docs.rs/backends/index.html)
- Backend registry. Per-target dispatch sits in `Registry::render`; backends themselves are feature-gated so a consumer can build with only what they need.
- [brand](https://docs.rs/brand/index.html)
- Brand specification: single source of truth for palette, fonts, margins, and the auto-layout rules. v1 only models what the page-layout system needs; richer projection (palette → typst/CSS/reference docs) lands in Phase 4.
- [images](https://docs.rs/images/index.html)
- Resolve markdown image references through the `AssetProvider`.
- [pages](https://docs.rs/pages/index.html)
- Page-aware IR for the doc body. Stage 1 (splitter) parses the surface
syntaxes into `RawPage`s; stage 2 (auto) assigns a`class`to produce`Page`s ready for backends.
- [preprocessor](https://docs.rs/preprocessor/index.html)
- User-pluggable markdown preprocessor.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Asset](https://docs.rs/struct.AssetRef.html)- Ref
- Reference to an external asset that the renderer should resolve via the
`AssetProvider`(e.g. an SVG rendered from a Mermaid pre-step).
- [Brand](https://docs.rs/struct.BrandHandle.html)- Handle
- Opaque handle into a `BrandSpec`so backends don’t carry the whole spec around.
- [DocMeta](https://docs.rs/struct.DocMeta.html)
- Document-level metadata extracted from frontmatter / config.
- [Render](https://docs.rs/struct.RenderRequest.html)- Request
- Per-render input passed to every backend. Holds the doc, the asset provider, and the destination path. Borrowed so the renderer never owns runtime state.
- [Resolved](https://docs.rs/struct.ResolvedDoc.html)- Doc
- The pipeline currency. OUR type — never pandoc’s AST.

# ws2812-rmt

A minimal, `no_std` WS2812/NeoPixel driver over `esp-hal`'s RMT peripheral —
no third-party `smart-leds`/RMT abstraction in between.

## Why this exists

Extracted from real-hardware debugging on an ESP32-C6
([ jcmendez/fall_sensor-rust](https://github.com/jcmendez/fall_sensor-rust))
after

[proved unable to reliably update a WS2812 pixel to a](https://crates.io/crates/esp-hal-smartled2)

`esp-hal-smartled2`*changing*value on repeated writes — a single steady color always rendered correctly, but blink/breathe patterns (i.e. anything other than "set it once and leave it") reliably corrupted: either sticking on a stale frame, or bleeding a previously-sent channel's value into later frames (a once-used blue value would visibly tint every later color — red became pink, green became cyan).

Root cause: that crate — like most WS2812/RMT drivers, including an earlier
version of this one — relies on the RMT channel's idle-low state *between*
separate transmissions to serve as the WS2812's required ≥50µs reset/latch
pulse, rather than encoding that reset explicitly in the transmitted buffer
the way Espressif's own reference encoder
([ esp-idf/examples/peripherals/rmt/led_strip_simple_encoder](https://github.com/espressif/esp-idf/blob/master/examples/peripherals/rmt/led_strip_simple_encoder/main/led_strip_example_main.c))
does. This crate always appends an explicit reset pulse, and transmits in

**blocking**mode (

`Channel::transmit(..).wait()`, which busy-polls hardware
status registers — no interrupt/async-waker path at all) so a bug in an
async completion path can't be a variable either.Full debugging writeup:
[ jcmendez/alerter_o1space_rust's doc/learnings.md](https://github.com/jcmendez/alerter_o1space_rust/blob/main/doc/learnings.md)
(search "WS2812").

## RMT clock tick period is chip- and configuration-specific — verify it

Every `Timing` field is a count of RMT clock *ticks*, not nanoseconds. The
tick period depends on your chip's RMT clock source (which varies by chip
family, and isn't always what `esp-hal`'s own metadata suggests — this crate
exists partly *because* that assumption was wrong once already) and on
`Rmt::new`'s requested frequency.

`Timing::WS2812_AT_12_5NS_TICK` is confirmed correct on an ESP32-C6 with:

```
let rmt = new?;
```
in your own setup code (this crate fixes the *channel's* additional clock
divider internally to reproduce the same recipe). If you're on a different
chip or clock configuration, verify on real hardware — a logic analyzer is
the reliable way. Empirically, a wrong tick period here doesn't fail loudly;
it renders as anything from "stuck on one color" to "completely dark".

## Usage

```
use ;
let rmt = new?;
let mut led =  buffer_len }>new?;
led.write?;
```
For more than one pixel, size the buffer for however many you have:

```
const PIXELS: usize = 25;
let mut leds =  buffer_len }>new?;
leds.write?;
```
## Chip support

Gated behind Cargo features matching `esp-hal`'s own chip features — enable
the one matching your target:

`esp32`, `esp32c2`, `esp32c3`, `esp32c5`, `esp32c6`, `esp32c61`, `esp32h2`,
`esp32s2`, `esp32s3`.

CI only exercises `esp32c3`/`esp32c6` (RISC-V targets installable via plain
`rustup`, no Xtensa toolchain needed) — the others should work by the same
`esp-hal` feature-forwarding mechanism, but haven't been build-tested here.

Licensed under either of

- Apache License, Version 2.0 ([LICENSE-APACHE](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-APACHE))
- MIT license ([LICENSE-MIT](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-MIT))

at your option.

# mr60fda2_proto - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/mr60fda2-proto/0.1.0/mr60fda2_proto/

Opt in to unsolicited HEIGHT_UPLOAD_TYPE (0x0E0E) frames – the sensor
does not stream live target height unless this is sent first (mirrors
controller.yaml’s boot-time uart.write).

RESULT_PARAMETERS (0x0E06) query – request the sensor’s current
install height / height threshold / sensitivity. The response comes back
as a ParseEvent::Parameters frame.

Set the fall-height threshold (RESULT_HEIGHT_THRESHOLD, 0x0E08).
index picks a value from HEIGHT_THRESHOLD_M. Ack arrives as
ParseEvent::SetHeightThresholdAck.

Set the mounting height (RESULT_INSTALL_HEIGHT, 0x0E04). index picks
a value from INSTALL_HEIGHT_M; returns None for an out-of-range
index. Ack arrives as ParseEvent::SetInstallHeightAck.

# option-operations 0.6.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/option-operations/0.6.1

# option-operations

`option-operations` provides traits and auto-implementations to
improve arithmetic operations usability when dealing with `Option`s.

## Example

Dealing with two `Option`s, can lead to verbose expressions:

```
let lhs = Some;
let rhs = Some;
assert_eq!;
```
Thanks to the trait `OptionSaturatingAdd` we can write:

```
assert_eq!;
```
The trait can also be used with the inner type:

```
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
```
## Alternative to `PartialOrd` for `Option<T>`

Another purpose is to workaround the `PartiaOrd` implementation
for `Option<T>`, which uses the declaration order of the variants
for `Option`. `None` appearing before `Some(_)`, it results in
the following behavior:

```
let some_0 = Some;
let none:  = None;
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
```
In some cases, we might consider that `None` reflects a value which
is not defined and thus can not be compared with `Some(_)`.

```
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
```
Of course, this is consistent with other usual comparisons:

```
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
```

- Apache License, Version 2.0, ([LICENSE-APACHE](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-APACHE)or[http://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0](http://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0))
- MIT license ([LICENSE-MIT](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-MIT)or[http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT](http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT))

# option_operations - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/option-operations/0.6.1/target-redirect/option_operations/

## Expand description

`option-operations` provides traits and auto-implementations to
improve arithmetic operations usability when dealing with `Option`s.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Dealing with two `Option`s, can lead to verbose expressions:

```
let lhs = Some(1u64);
let rhs = Some(u64::MAX);
assert_eq!(
    lhs.zip(rhs).map(|(lhs, rhs)| lhs.saturating_add(rhs)),
    Some(u64::MAX),
);
```
Thanks to the trait [ OptionSaturatingAdd](https://docs.rs/add/trait.OptionSaturatingAdd.html) we can write:

```
assert_eq!(
    lhs.opt_saturating_add(rhs),
    Some(u64::MAX),
);
```
The trait can also be used with the inner type:

```
assert_eq!(
    lhs.opt_saturating_add(u64::MAX),
    Some(u64::MAX),
);
assert_eq!(
    1.opt_saturating_add(rhs),
    Some(u64::MAX),
);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#alternative-to-partialord-for-optiont)Alternative to `PartialOrd` for `Option<T>`

Another purpose is to workaround the `PartiaOrd` implementation
for `Option<T>`, which uses the declaration order of the variants
for `Option`. `None` appearing before `Some(_)`, it results in
the following behavior:

```
let some_0 = Some(0);
let none: Option<u64> = None;
assert_eq!(none.partial_cmp(&some_0), Some(Ordering::Less));
assert_eq!(some_0.partial_cmp(&none), Some(Ordering::Greater));
```
In some cases, we might consider that `None` reflects a value which
is not defined and thus can not be compared with `Some(_)`.

```
assert_eq!(none.opt_cmp(&some_0), None);
assert_eq!(some_0.opt_cmp(&none), None);
```
Of course, this is consistent with other usual comparisons:

```
assert_eq!(none.opt_lt(&some_0), None);
assert_eq!(none.opt_min(some_0), None);
```

# lib.rs - source

Source: https://docs.rs/option-operations/0.6.1/src/option_operations/lib.rs.html

# option_operations/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! `option-operations` provides traits and auto-implementations to
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//! improve arithmetic operations usability when dealing with `Option`s.
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//!
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//! # Example
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//!
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//! Dealing with two `Option`s, can lead to verbose expressions:
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//!
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//! ```
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! let lhs = Some(1u64);
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//! let rhs = Some(u64::MAX);
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//!
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//! assert_eq!(
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//!     lhs.zip(rhs).map(|(lhs, rhs)| lhs.saturating_add(rhs)),
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//!     Some(u64::MAX),
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! );
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//! ```
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//!
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//! Thanks to the trait [`OptionSaturatingAdd`] we can write:
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//!
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//! ```
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! # use option_operations::{Error, OptionSaturatingAdd};
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//! # let lhs = Some(1u64);
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//! # let rhs = Some(u64::MAX);
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//! assert_eq!(
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//!     lhs.opt_saturating_add(rhs),
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//!     Some(u64::MAX),
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//! );
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//! ```
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//!
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//! The trait can also be used with the inner type:
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//!
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//! ```
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//! # use option_operations::{Error, OptionSaturatingAdd};
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//! # let lhs = Some(1u64);
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//! # let rhs = Some(u64::MAX);
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//! assert_eq!(
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//!     lhs.opt_saturating_add(u64::MAX),
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//!     Some(u64::MAX),
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//! );
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//!
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//! assert_eq!(
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//!     1.opt_saturating_add(rhs),
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//!     Some(u64::MAX),
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//! );
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//! ```
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//!
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//! # Alternative to `PartialOrd` for `Option<T>`
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//!
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//! Another purpose is to workaround the `PartiaOrd` implementation
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//! for `Option<T>`, which uses the declaration order of the variants
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//! for `Option`. `None` appearing before `Some(_)`, it results in
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//! the following behavior:
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//!
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//! ```
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//! # use core::cmp::Ordering;
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//! let some_0 = Some(0);
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//! let none: Option<u64> = None;
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//!
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//! assert_eq!(none.partial_cmp(&some_0), Some(Ordering::Less));
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//! assert_eq!(some_0.partial_cmp(&none), Some(Ordering::Greater));
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//! ```
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//!
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//! In some cases, we might consider that `None` reflects a value which
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//! is not defined and thus can not be compared with `Some(_)`.
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//!
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//! ```
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//! # use option_operations::{OptionOperations, OptionOrd};
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//! # let some_0 = Some(0);
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//! # let none: Option<u64> = None;
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//! assert_eq!(none.opt_cmp(&some_0), None);
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//! assert_eq!(some_0.opt_cmp(&none), None);
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//! ```
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//!
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//! Of course, this is consistent with other usual comparisons:
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//!
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//! ``` rust
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//! # use option_operations::{OptionOperations, OptionOrd, OptionMinMax};
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//! # let some_0 = Some(0);
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//! # let none: Option<u64> = None;
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//! assert_eq!(none.opt_lt(&some_0), None);
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//! assert_eq!(none.opt_min(some_0), None);
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//! ```
[83](https://docs.rs#83)
[84](https://docs.rs#84)#![forbid(unsafe_code)]
[85](https://docs.rs#85)#![cfg_attr(not(feature = "std"), no_std)]
[86](https://docs.rs#86)
[87](https://docs.rs#87)/// Trait for inner types participating in `option-operations`.
[88](https://docs.rs#88)///
[89](https://docs.rs#89)/// The purpose of this trait is twofold:
[90](https://docs.rs#90)///
[91](https://docs.rs#91)/// - Auto-implement various `Option*` traits such as `OptionOrd`.
[92](https://docs.rs#92)/// - Prevent some conflicting auto-implementation of traits on
[93](https://docs.rs#93)///   `Option<T>`.
[94](https://docs.rs#94)pub trait OptionOperations {}
[95](https://docs.rs#95)

[97](https://docs.rs#97)impl<T: OptionOperations> OptionOperations for &mut T {}
[98](https://docs.rs#98)

# OptionSaturatingAdd in option_operations::add - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/option-operations/0.6.1/option_operations/add/trait.OptionSaturatingAdd.html

```
pub trait OptionSaturatingAdd<Rhs = Self, InnerRhs = Rhs> {
    type
```
[Output](https://docs.rs#associatedtype.Output);
    // Required method
    fn [opt_saturating_add](https://docs.rs#tymethod.opt_saturating_add)(self, rhs: Rhs) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<Self::[Output](https://docs.rs/trait.OptionSaturatingAdd.html#associatedtype.Output)>;
}## Expand description

Trait for values and `Option`s saturating addition.

Implementing this trait leads to the following auto-implementations:

- `OptionSaturatingAdd<Option<InnerRhs>>`for- `T`.
- `OptionSaturatingAdd<Rhs>`for- `Option<T>`.
- `OptionSaturatingAdd<Option<InnerRhs>>`for- `Option<T>`.
- … and some variants with references.

Note that since the `std` library doesn’t define any
`SaturatingAdd` trait,
users must provide the base implementation for the inner type.

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

#### fn [opt_overflowing_add](https://docs.rs#tymethod.opt_overflowing_add)(self, rhs: Rhs) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<(Self::[Output](https://docs.rs/trait.OptionOverflowingAdd.html#associatedtype.Output), [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html))>

Returns a tuple of the addition
along with a boolean indicating whether an arithmetic overflow
would occur. If an overflow would have occurred then `self` is returned.

Returns `None` if at least one argument is `None`.

# OptionCheckedDiv in option_operations::div - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/option-operations/0.6.1/option_operations/div/trait.OptionCheckedDiv.html

```
pub trait OptionCheckedDiv<Rhs = Self, InnerRhs = Rhs> {
    type
```
[Output](https://docs.rs#associatedtype.Output);
    // Required method
    fn [opt_checked_div](https://docs.rs#tymethod.opt_checked_div)(self, rhs: Rhs) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<Self::[Output](https://docs.rs/trait.OptionCheckedDiv.html#associatedtype.Output)>, [Error](https://docs.rs/error/enum.Error.html)>;
}## Expand description

Trait for values and `Option`s checked division.

Implementing this trait leads to the following auto-implementations:

- `OptionCheckedDiv<Option<InnerRhs>>`for- `T`.
- `OptionCheckedDiv<Rhs>`for- `Option<T>`.
- `OptionCheckedDiv<Option<InnerRhs>>`for- `Option<T>`.
- … and some variants with references.

Note that since the `std` library doesn’t define any
`CheckedDiv` trait,
users must provide the base implementation for the inner type.

## Required Associated Types[§](https://docs.rs#required-associated-types)

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

Computes the checked division.

- Returns `Ok(Some(result))`if`result`could be computed.
- Returns `Ok(None)`if at least one argument is`None`.
- Returns `Err(Error::Overflow)`if an overflow occured.
- Returns `Err(Error::DivisionByZero)`if`rhs`is zero.

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait **is** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

along with a boolean indicating whether an arithmetic overflow

# OptionOrd in option_operations::ord - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/option-operations/0.6.1/option_operations/ord/trait.OptionOrd.html

```
pub trait OptionOrd<Rhs, InnerRhs = Rhs> {
    // Required method
    fn
```
[opt_cmp](https://docs.rs#tymethod.opt_cmp)(&self, rhs: Rhs) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[Ordering](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/enum.Ordering.html)>;
    // Provided methods
    fn [opt_lt](https://docs.rs#method.opt_lt)(&self, rhs: Rhs) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)> { ... }
[opt_le](https://docs.rs#method.opt_le)(&self, rhs: Rhs) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)> { ... }
[opt_gt](https://docs.rs#method.opt_gt)(&self, rhs: Rhs) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)> { ... }
[opt_ge](https://docs.rs#method.opt_ge)(&self, rhs: Rhs) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)> { ... }
}## Expand description

Trait for values and `Option`s that can be compared for a sort-order.

This implementation is mainly intended at working around the `PartialOrd`
implementation for `Option`, which compares `Option`s
depending on the order of declaration in the `enum`.

[§](https://docs.rs#partialord-implementation-for-option)`PartialOrd` implementation for `Option`

```
let some_0 = Some(0);
let none: Option<u64> = None;
assert_eq!(none.partial_cmp(&some_0), Some(Ordering::Less));
assert_eq!(some_0.partial_cmp(&none), Some(Ordering::Greater));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#alternative-behavior)Alternative behavior

In some cases, we might consider that `None` reflects a value which
is not defined and thus can not be compared with `Some(_)`.

```
assert_eq!(none.opt_cmp(&some_0), None);
assert_eq!(some_0.opt_cmp(&none), None);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#implementations-1)Implementations

Implementing this type leads to the following auto-implementations:

- `OptionOrd<Option<InnerRhs>> for T`.
- `OptionOrd<Rhs> for Option<T>`.
- `OptionOrd<Option<InnerRhs>> for Option<T>`.
- … and some variants with references.

This trait is auto-implemented for [ OptionOperations](https://docs.rs/trait.OptionOperations.html) types
implementing

`PartialOrd<Rhs>`.## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

Tests whether `self` is less than `rhs`.

Returns `None` if they can’t be compared, e.g. if
at most one argument is `None`.

Tests whether `self` is less or equal to `rhs`.

Returns `None` if they can’t be compared, e.g. if
at most one argument is `None`.

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait **is** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

---

- `OptionOverflowingRem<Option<InnerRhs>>`for- `Option<T>`.
- … and some variants with references.

Note that since the `std` library doesn’t define any
`OverflowingRem` trait,
users must provide the base implementation for the inner type.

## Required Associated Types[§](https://docs.rs#required-associated-types)

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/option_operations/rem.rs.html#7-16)#### fn [opt_overflowing_rem](https://docs.rs#tymethod.opt_overflowing_rem)(self, rhs: Rhs) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<(Self::[Output](https://docs.rs/trait.OptionOverflowingRem.html#associatedtype.Output), [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html))>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/option_operations/rem.rs.html#7-16)

#### fn [opt_overflowing_rem](https://docs.rs#tymethod.opt_overflowing_rem)(self, rhs: Rhs) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<(Self::[Output](https://docs.rs/trait.OptionOverflowingRem.html#associatedtype.Output), [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html))>

Returns a tuple of the remainder
along with a boolean indicating whether an arithmetic overflow
would occur. If an overflow would have occurred then `self` is returned.

Returns `None` if at least one argument is `None`.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

Most implementations will panic if `rhs` is zero.

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait **is** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

---

# OptionOperations in option_operations - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/option-operations/0.6.1/option_operations/trait.OptionOperations.html

`pub trait OptionOperations { }`## Expand description

Trait for inner types participating in `option-operations`.

The purpose of this trait is twofold:

- Auto-implement various `Option*`traits such as`OptionOrd`.
- Prevent some conflicting auto-implementation of traits on
`Option<T>`.

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait **is** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# option_operations - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/option-operations/latest/option_operations/

## Expand description

`option-operations` provides traits and auto-implementations to
improve arithmetic operations usability when dealing with `Option`s.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Dealing with two `Option`s, can lead to verbose expressions:

```
let lhs = Some(1u64);
let rhs = Some(u64::MAX);
assert_eq!(
    lhs.zip(rhs).map(|(lhs, rhs)| lhs.saturating_add(rhs)),
    Some(u64::MAX),
);
```
Thanks to the trait [ OptionSaturatingAdd](https://docs.rs/add/trait.OptionSaturatingAdd.html) we can write:

```
assert_eq!(
    lhs.opt_saturating_add(rhs),
    Some(u64::MAX),
);
```
The trait can also be used with the inner type:

```
assert_eq!(
    lhs.opt_saturating_add(u64::MAX),
    Some(u64::MAX),
);
assert_eq!(
    1.opt_saturating_add(rhs),
    Some(u64::MAX),
);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#alternative-to-partialord-for-optiont)Alternative to `PartialOrd` for `Option<T>`

Another purpose is to workaround the `PartiaOrd` implementation
for `Option<T>`, which uses the declaration order of the variants
for `Option`. `None` appearing before `Some(_)`, it results in
the following behavior:

```
let some_0 = Some(0);
let none: Option<u64> = None;
assert_eq!(none.partial_cmp(&some_0), Some(Ordering::Less));
assert_eq!(some_0.partial_cmp(&none), Some(Ordering::Greater));
```
In some cases, we might consider that `None` reflects a value which
is not defined and thus can not be compared with `Some(_)`.

```
assert_eq!(none.opt_cmp(&some_0), None);
assert_eq!(some_0.opt_cmp(&none), None);
```
Of course, this is consistent with other usual comparisons:

```
assert_eq!(none.opt_lt(&some_0), None);
assert_eq!(none.opt_min(some_0), None);
```

All the builds on docs.rs are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The limits for this crate are the following:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                    If a build fails because it hit one of those limits please
                    [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                    to get them increased.

# pastey 0.2.3 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/pastey/^0.2.0

# Macros for all your token pasting needs

`pastey` is the fork of `paste` and is aimed to be a drop-in replacement with additional features for
`paste` crate

Migrating from `paste` crate to `pastey` is super simple, just change the following
in your `Cargo.toml`

```
[dependencies]
- paste = "1"
+ pastey = "*" # Or any specific version of pastey
```
Or even better way:

```
[dependencies]
- paste = "1"
+ paste = { package = "pastey", version = "*" }
```
## Quick Start

Add `pastey` as your dependency in `Cargo.toml`

```
[]
# TODO: Replace with latest version available on crates.io
 = "*"
```
This approach works with any Rust compiler 1.54+.

## Pasting identifiers

Within the `paste!` macro, identifiers inside `[<`...`>]` are pasted together to
form a single identifier.

```
use paste;
paste!
```
## More elaborate example

The next example shows a macro that generates accessor methods for some struct fields. It demonstrates how you might find it useful to bundle a paste invocation inside of a macro_rules macro.

```
use paste;
    }
}
make_a_struct_and_getters!;
let s = S ;
 assert!;
 let s2 = S ;
 assert!;
```
## Case conversion

The `pastey` crate supports the following case modfiers:

| Modifier | Description |
|---|---|
| `$var:lower` | Lower Case |
| `$var:upper` | Upper Case |
| `$var:snake` | Snake Case |
| `$var:camel`or`$var:upper_camel` | Upper Camel Case |
| `$var:lower_camel` | Lower Camel Case [#4](https://github.com/AS1100K/pastey/issues/4) |
| `$var:camel_edge` | Covers Edge cases of Camel Case. [#3](https://github.com/AS1100K/pastey/issues/3) |

**NOTE: The pastey crate is going to be a drop in replacement to paste crate,
and will not change the behaviour of existing modifier like  lower, upper,
snake and camel. For modifying the behaviour new modifiers will be created,
like camel_edge**

You can also use multiple of these modifers like `$var:snake:upper` would give you
`SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE`.

Example

```
use paste;
paste!
```
The precise Unicode conversions are as defined by [ str::to_lowercase](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html#method.to_lowercase) and

[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html#method.to_uppercase)

`str::to_uppercase`## Replace modifier

The `replace` modifier allows you to perform string replacement on identifiers,
using the same semantics as [ str::replace](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html#method.replace). This is useful for transforming
identifiers by removing or substituting substrings.

```
use paste;
        }
    }
}
m!
let command_bar = Bar;
let command_foo = Foo;
let command_hello = World;
```
## Raw Identifier Generation

`pastey` now supports raw identifiers using a special raw mode. By prefixing a
token with `#` inside the paste syntax, it treats that token as a raw identifier.

```
use paste;
define_struct_and_impl!;
define_struct_and_impl!;
test_fn;
```
## Pasting documentation strings

Within the `paste!` macro, arguments to a #[doc ...] attribute are implicitly
concatenated together to form a coherent documentation string.

```
use paste;
method_new!;  // expands to #[doc = "Create a new `Paste` object"]
let _ = new;
```

---

# option-operations 0.6.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/option-operations/0.6.0

# option-operations

`option-operations` provides traits and auto-implementations to
improve arithmetic operations usability when dealing with `Option`s.

## Example

Dealing with two `Option`s, can lead to verbose expressions:

```
let lhs = Some;
let rhs = Some;
assert_eq!;
```
Thanks to the trait `OptionSaturatingAdd` we can write:

```
assert_eq!;
```
The trait can also be used with the inner type:

```
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
```
## Alternative to `PartialOrd` for `Option<T>`

Another purpose is to workaround the `PartiaOrd` implementation
for `Option<T>`, which uses the declaration order of the variants
for `Option`. `None` appearing before `Some(_)`, it results in
the following behavior:

```
let some_0 = Some;
let none:  = None;
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
```
In some cases, we might consider that `None` reflects a value which
is not defined and thus can not be compared with `Some(_)`.

```
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
```
Of course, this is consistent with other usual comparisons:

```
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
```

# option_operations - Rust

## Expand description

improve arithmetic operations usability when dealing with `Option`s.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Dealing with two `Option`s, can lead to verbose expressions:

```
let lhs = Some(1u64);
let rhs = Some(u64::MAX);
assert_eq!(
    lhs.zip(rhs).map(|(lhs, rhs)| lhs.saturating_add(rhs)),
    Some(u64::MAX),
);
```
Thanks to the trait [ OptionSaturatingAdd](https://docs.rs/add/trait.OptionSaturatingAdd.html) we can write:

```
assert_eq!(
    lhs.opt_saturating_add(rhs),
    Some(u64::MAX),
);
```
The trait can also be used with the inner type:

```
assert_eq!(
    lhs.opt_saturating_add(u64::MAX),
    Some(u64::MAX),
);
assert_eq!(
    1.opt_saturating_add(rhs),
    Some(u64::MAX),
);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#alternative-to-partialord-for-optiont)Alternative to `PartialOrd` for `Option<T>`

Another purpose is to workaround the `PartiaOrd` implementation
for `Option<T>`, which uses the declaration order of the variants
for `Option`. `None` appearing before `Some(_)`, it results in
the following behavior:

```
let some_0 = Some(0);
let none: Option<u64> = None;
assert_eq!(none.partial_cmp(&some_0), Some(Ordering::Less));
assert_eq!(some_0.partial_cmp(&none), Some(Ordering::Greater));
```
In some cases, we might consider that `None` reflects a value which
is not defined and thus can not be compared with `Some(_)`.

```
assert_eq!(none.opt_cmp(&some_0), None);
assert_eq!(some_0.opt_cmp(&none), None);
```
Of course, this is consistent with other usual comparisons:

```
assert_eq!(none.opt_lt(&some_0), None);
assert_eq!(none.opt_min(some_0), None);
```

##[0.6.0] -- 2025-09-01###Changed-Use `pastey` instead of `paste` which is no longer maintained.
This also requires upgrading the MSRV to 1.54.
##[0.5.0] -- 2022-08-15###Fixed-Fix `prelude` not exporting `OptionEq`.
##[0.4.1] -- 2022-06-29###Added-Fix repository link in `Cargo.toml`.
- Specify Minimum Supported Rust Version.
###Fixed-Error: fix a typo in Display impl.
###Changed-Add `forbid(unsafe_code)` constraint.
##[0.4.0] -- 2021-10-24###Fixed-Fix auto implementations for OptionOp and OptionOpAssign. In previous version
all the implementations required that Op & OpAssign be implemented, which was
not consistent with documentation and other Option* traits. Now, the user can
implement OptionOp and OptionOpAssign on the inner type and automatically
benefit from the implementations on the other variations.
###Changed-Factorize code in macros.
##[0.3.0] -- 2021-10-18###Changed-**Breaking**: don't export internal macros.
##[0.2.0] -- 2021-10-15###Added-#[must_use] attributes where applicable.
- Documentation for the associated types.
##[0.1.0] -- 2021-10-07-First version with the most common operations.

# pastey 0.2.3 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/pastey/0.2.3

# Macros for all your token pasting needs

`pastey` is the fork of `paste` and is aimed to be a drop-in replacement with additional features for
`paste` crate

Migrating from `paste` crate to `pastey` is super simple, just change the following
in your `Cargo.toml`

```
[dependencies]
- paste = "1"
+ pastey = "*" # Or any specific version of pastey
```
Or even better way:

```
[dependencies]
- paste = "1"
+ paste = { package = "pastey", version = "*" }
```
## Quick Start

Add `pastey` as your dependency in `Cargo.toml`

```
[]
# TODO: Replace with latest version available on crates.io
 = "*"
```
This approach works with any Rust compiler 1.54+.

## Pasting identifiers

Within the `paste!` macro, identifiers inside `[<`...`>]` are pasted together to
form a single identifier.

```
use paste;
paste!
```
## More elaborate example

The next example shows a macro that generates accessor methods for some struct fields. It demonstrates how you might find it useful to bundle a paste invocation inside of a macro_rules macro.

```
use paste;
    }
}
make_a_struct_and_getters!;
let s = S ;
 assert!;
 let s2 = S ;
 assert!;
```
## Case conversion

The `pastey` crate supports the following case modfiers:

| Modifier | Description |
|---|---|
| `$var:lower` | Lower Case |
| `$var:upper` | Upper Case |
| `$var:snake` | Snake Case |
| `$var:camel`or`$var:upper_camel` | Upper Camel Case |
| `$var:lower_camel` | Lower Camel Case [#4](https://github.com/AS1100K/pastey/issues/4) |
| `$var:camel_edge` | Covers Edge cases of Camel Case. [#3](https://github.com/AS1100K/pastey/issues/3) |

**NOTE: The pastey crate is going to be a drop in replacement to paste crate,
and will not change the behaviour of existing modifier like  lower, upper,
snake and camel. For modifying the behaviour new modifiers will be created,
like camel_edge**

You can also use multiple of these modifers like `$var:snake:upper` would give you
`SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE`.

Example

```
use paste;
paste!
```
The precise Unicode conversions are as defined by [ str::to_lowercase](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html#method.to_lowercase) and

[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html#method.to_uppercase)

`str::to_uppercase`## Replace modifier

The `replace` modifier allows you to perform string replacement on identifiers,
using the same semantics as [ str::replace](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html#method.replace). This is useful for transforming
identifiers by removing or substituting substrings.

```
use paste;
        }
    }
}
m!
let command_bar = Bar;
let command_foo = Foo;
let command_hello = World;
```
## Raw Identifier Generation

`pastey` now supports raw identifiers using a special raw mode. By prefixing a
token with `#` inside the paste syntax, it treats that token as a raw identifier.

```
use paste;
define_struct_and_impl!;
define_struct_and_impl!;
test_fn;
```
## Pasting documentation strings

Within the `paste!` macro, arguments to a #[doc ...] attribute are implicitly
concatenated together to form a coherent documentation string.

```
use paste;
method_new!;  // expands to #[doc = "Create a new `Paste` object"]
let _ = new;
```

# pastey - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/pastey/0.2.3/target-redirect/pastey/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#macros-for-all-your-token-pasting-needs)Macros for all your token pasting needs

`pastey` is the fork of `paste` and is aimed to be a drop-in replacement with additional features for
`paste` crate

## Migrating from `paste` crate

Migrating from `paste` crate to `pastey` is super simple, just change the following
in your `Cargo.toml`

```
[dependencies]
- paste = "1"
+ pastey = "*" # Or any specific version of pastey
```
Or even better way:

```
[dependencies]
- paste = "1"
+ paste = { package = "pastey", version = "*" }
```
[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

Add `pastey` as your dependency in `Cargo.toml`

```
[dependencies]
# TODO: Replace with latest version available on crates.io
pastey = "*"
```
This approach works with any Rust compiler 1.54+.

[§](https://docs.rs#pasting-identifiers)Pasting identifiers

Within the `paste!` macro, identifiers inside `[<`…`>]` are pasted together to
form a single identifier.

```
use pastey::paste;
paste! {
    // Defines a const called `QRST`.
    const [<Q R S T>]: &str = "success!";
}
fn main() {
    assert_eq!(
        paste! { [<Q R S T>].len() },
        8,
    );
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#more-elaborate-example)More elaborate example

The next example shows a macro that generates accessor methods for some struct fields. It demonstrates how you might find it useful to bundle a paste invocation inside of a macro_rules macro.

```
use pastey::paste;
macro_rules! make_a_struct_and_getters {
    ($name:ident { $($field:ident),* }) => {
        // Define a struct. This expands to:
        //
        //     pub struct S {
        //         a: String,
        //         b: String,
        //         c: String,
        //     }
        pub struct $name {
            $(
                $field: String,
            )*
        }
        // Build an impl block with getters. This expands to:
        //
        //     impl S {
        //         pub fn get_a(&self) -> &str { &self.a }
        //         pub fn get_b(&self) -> &str { &self.b }
        //         pub fn get_c(&self) -> &str { &self.c }
        //     }
        paste! {
            impl $name {
                $(
                    pub fn [<get_ $field>](&self) -> &str {
                        &self.$field
                    }
                )*
            }
        }
    }
}
make_a_struct_and_getters!(S { a, b, c });
fn call_some_getters(s: &S) -> bool {
    s.get_a() == s.get_b() && s.get_c().is_empty()
}
let s = S {
    a: String::from("x"),
    b: String::from("x"),
    c: String::new(),
 };
 assert!(call_some_getters(&s));
 let s2 = S {
     a: String::from("x"),
     b: String::from("y"),
     c: String::new(),
 };
 assert!(!call_some_getters(&s2));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#case-conversion)Case conversion

The `pastey` crate supports the following case modfiers:

| Modifier | Description |
|---|---|
| `$var:lower` | Lower Case |
| `$var:upper` | Upper Case |
| `$var:snake` | Snake Case |
| `$var:camel`or`$var:upper_camel` | Upper Camel Case |
| `$var:lower_camel` | Lower Camel Case [#4](https://github.com/AS1100K/pastey/issues/4) |
| `$var:camel_edge` | Covers Edge cases of Camel Case. [#3](https://github.com/AS1100K/pastey/issues/3) |

**NOTE: The pastey crate is going to be a drop in replacement to paste crate,
and will not change the behaviour of existing modifier like  lower, upper,
snake and camel. For modifying the behaviour new modifiers will be created,
like camel_edge**

You can also use multiple of these modifers like `$var:snake:upper` would give you
`SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE`.

Example

```
use pastey::paste;
paste! {
    const [<LIB env!("CARGO_PKG_NAME"):snake:upper>]: &str = "libpastey";
    let _ = LIBPASTEY;
}
```
The precise Unicode conversions are as defined by [ str::to_lowercase](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html#method.to_lowercase) and

[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html#method.to_uppercase)

`str::to_uppercase`[§](https://docs.rs#replace-modifier)Replace modifier

The `replace` modifier allows you to perform string replacement on identifiers,
using the same semantics as [ str::replace](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.str.html#method.replace). This is useful for transforming
identifiers by removing or substituting substrings.

```
use pastey::paste;
macro_rules! m {
    ($(($command:ident, $from:ident)),+) => {
        paste! {
            $(pub struct $command {})*
            pub enum Command {
                $(
                    [< $command:replace($from, "") >] ( $command )
                ),*
            }
        }
    }
}
m! {
    (CommandFoo, Command),
    (CommandBar, Command),
    (HelloWorld, Hello)
}
let command_bar = Command::Bar(CommandBar {});
let command_foo = Command::Foo(CommandFoo {});
let command_hello = Command::World(HelloWorld {});
```
[§](https://docs.rs#raw-identifier-generation)Raw Identifier Generation

`pastey` now supports raw identifiers using a special raw mode. By prefixing a
token with `#` inside the paste syntax, it treats that token as a raw identifier.

```
use pastey::paste;
macro_rules! define_struct_and_impl {
    ($name:ident $(- $name_tail:ident)*) => {
        paste!{
            struct [< # $name:camel $( $name_tail)* >]; // '#' signals a raw identifier
            impl [< # $name:camel $( $name_tail)* >] {
                fn [< # $name:snake $( _ $name_tail:snake)* >]() {}
            }
        }
    }
}
define_struct_and_impl!(loop);
define_struct_and_impl!(loop - xyz);
fn test_fn() {
    let _ = Loop::r#loop();
    let _ = Loopxyz::loop_xyz();
}
test_fn();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#pasting-documentation-strings)Pasting documentation strings

Within the `paste!` macro, arguments to a #[doc …] attribute are implicitly
concatenated together to form a coherent documentation string.

```
use pastey::paste;
macro_rules! method_new {
    ($ret:ident) => {
        paste! {
            #[doc = "Create a new `" $ret "` object."]
            pub fn new() -> $ret { $ret {} }
        }
    };
}
pub struct Pastey {}
method_new!(Pastey);  // expands to #[doc = "Create a new `Paste` object"]
let _ = new();
```
